chunks: From him, from Ibn Faddal, from Muthanna, from Hatim ibn Ismail al-Madaini, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The foundling is free (i.e., has the right to choose his own guardian); if he wishes, he may be accompanied by someone other than the one who raised and nourished him. And if the one who raised him seeks maintenance from him, and he is wealthy, he must pay him; but if he is poor, what he spends on him is considered charity.

key_terms.النَّفَقَةَ: Maintenance; financial support provided to the dependent.
key_terms.الْمَنْبُوذُ: The foundling; a child found abandoned whose lineage is unknown.
key_terms.حُرٌّ: Free; possessing autonomy, specifically here to choose a guardian.
key_terms.رَبَّاهُ: He who raised and nurtured the child.
key_terms.صَدَقَةً: Charity; a voluntary gift rather than an obligatory debt.
key_terms.مُيَسِّراً: Wealthy; having sufficient means to pay.
key_terms.يُوَالِيَ: To accompany or be under the guardianship/companionship of.

ai.seo_question: What are the rights and obligations of a foundling regarding guardianship and financial support in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In Shia jurisprudence, this hadith clarifies that a 'manbuth' (foundling) retains full freedom to choose his guardian rather than being bound to his raiser, distinguishing between obligatory support and voluntary charity. It establishes that financial maintenance is contingent upon the raiser's wealth; if he is affluent, the foundling must provide support, but if he is poor, the support given is considered *sadaqah* (voluntary charity). This ruling underscores the flexibility in familial obligations and the merit of charity within the Shia legal tradition.
